subjects.displayTitle: Influence and centrality of the Word of God
subjects.introduction: What is the Word of God, and why do the Writings place it at the centre of creation, revelation and the life of the soul? These 300 chosen quotations include every verified authorized selection in the compilation. They begin with the Word as the origin of creation and its station above all speech, then turn to the Book that speaks and to the verses offered as proof. They follow the Word as the water of life, its power to make souls new and to conquer hearts, and its gathering of the peoples. Later readings consider the conditions of hearing, the oceans of meaning within the words and what reading, reciting and acting ask of the believer, before turning to what endures and closing with prayers. Passages come from Bahá’u’lláh, the Báb and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá, with reported talks and secondary accounts among them; supplied wording follows at the end with its catalogue status.

The Báb testifies that God’s Word is His Command, through which all things stand, and that through a single word God creates whatever He wills. These readings ask what the Word of God is. Bahá’u’lláh writes that it can never be confounded with the words of His creatures and is the King of words, that it is higher than what the senses perceive and sanctified from any substance, and that among human utterances the Divine Word is as the sun. The one revelation is called in one station the Word, in another the Will and in another the Divine Purpose, and God has made all words a throne for His Word. The Báb teaches that God has placed no intermediary between Himself and His chosen ones except His Word, the mirror that reflects its Speaker. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá and reported talks explain the opening of the Gospel of John, In the beginning was the Word, and the sense in which Christ was the Word. How can the Word be both the speech of God and the reality of the Manifestation? What follows from refusing to compare it with any other speech?

These readings present the verses as proof. Bahá’u’lláh writes that, compared with all other proofs and tokens, the divinely revealed verses shine as the sun, while all others are as stars, and He makes His verses a path unto His knowledge and the abiding testimony of His Revelation. He answers the objection that the verses have been made the standard of their own authenticity, and asks by what word faith could be established if this proof were denied. The Báb challenges all in heaven and earth to produce the like of a single verse, and asks what proof could be greater than one appearing in Persia and speaking in the language of the Qur’án. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá counts among the signs the eloquence and rapidity of the revelation and says each group takes its own portion of proof from the verses, which were revealed like torrential rain. Why should words be the greatest proof? How do the readings answer the charge that such a proof is circular?

These readings show souls made new. Bahá’u’lláh says that every letter proceeding from His mouth can bring into existence a new creation, that a shepherd became the guide of nations and a fisherman was endowed with divine wisdom, and that after His word the tongue-tied gained speech and the ignorant entered the ocean of knowledge. Reported talks add that philosophers are powerless without the Spirit and that the Word improves character. What changes in a person who is born of the Word? Why do the readings so often choose the humble as their examples?

These readings consider the hearer. The same verses, the Báb writes, are a light to those who believe and a fire to those who turn away, and Bahá’u’lláh says the believers quaff from them the wine of everlasting life while the ungodly drink a scalding draught. The penetrating influence of the Word depends upon the sanctification of the heart and emanates from its sincerity; the Pen flows only with what the people are capable of bearing, and today the station of the Word is concealed because of the people’s lack of capacity. Names and words have become veils. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá observes that oil ignites at once on touching fire while black stone does not, and reported talks apply Christ’s parable of the seed. Whoever gives ear to the Call is among the most distinguished souls, though a carrier of ashes. What makes a heart able to hear? Why do the same words heal one soul and harden another?

Those who attain the verses are to strive for deeds whose fragrance endures; had the loved ones acted on what the Pen revealed, most of the servants would have turned to God. Teaching the Cause is named the greatest of deeds, the Words of God are the keys to hearts, and the utterances of this Revelation are to be collected. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá praises a Sunday school where the Word of God is recited for children and promises eloquent utterance to whoever opens their tongue in teaching. How are reading, acting and teaching joined here? What does regard for the dignity of the Word ask?

These readings ask what endures. Bahá’u’lláh contrasts a world that came from nothingness and will return to nothingness with what lasts forever: the world will change, but the glory of the Divine Word will not, and whatever has flowed from the Pen will appear word for word. Whoever serves the Cause endures through the endurance of God’s Word, and every word uttered for God’s sake is like a tree whose leaves and fruits will appear. The Divine Tablet is a helper in life and death. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá bids the believers keep their attention on the Word of God and rejoice whenever it is ascendant, whatever befalls Him, and says that Bahá’u’lláh engraved His teachings on hearts like an engraving on stone. What gives a word permanence when written words can be effaced by water? How do these passages change the measure of what is worth doing?

The linked readings close with prayers. Bahá’u’lláh calls upon God by His most exalted Word, ordained as the Divine Elixir through whose potency the crude metal of human life is transmuted into purest gold, by the Word that is the king of all words, and by the word that has shone forth above the horizon of His will. He testifies that by a word of His mouth God has revolutionized the entire creation, gives thanks that the loved ones have been born again through the living waters flowing from the mouth of His will, and asks that the ears of the servants be purged to hear the sweet melodies of His throne. One prayer asks God to unseal the lips of His will and let a word proceed that shall subject the world to itself. What do these prayers ask the Word to do? How might they be used before reading the Writings?

The linked record renders the same paragraph provisionally and outside its authorized range, so the supplied wording keeps its approximate status. Compare it with the dewdrop that is the Primal Word in the opening readings. Why should so little suffice?

In this authorized invocation Bahá’u’lláh addresses God as the One the words of Whose mouth are as the waters of life unto all who are in heaven and on earth. The ellipsis passes over the attributes of God’s face, presence, nearness, name and voice that the full prayer names first; the approximate status is preserved. Read it with the readings on the water of life.

In this authorized sentence Bahá’u’lláh says that the Tongue of God testifies to the truth of His words through His own Word, which speaks the truth and embraces and comprehends all things. questions: The readings call the Word the origin of creation, the water of life and the master key to hearts. Choose one of these images and trace it through several sections. What does it show about the Word that the others do not?

Bahá’u’lláh writes that the verses shine among all proofs as the sun among the stars, yet also that the station of the Word is concealed because of the people’s lack of capacity. How can the same proof be manifest and hidden at once, and what do the readings say a seeker must bring?

Why do so many passages warn against pride in a Book, against resting in the outward meaning and against interpreting God’s words by one’s own desires? Compare the people of the Torah, the Furqán and the Bayán with those who immerse themselves in the ocean of meanings.
The law of the sword has been abolished and the law of utterance revealed. How do the readings describe the conquest of hearts, and what do they ask of believers who carry the Word to others?

‘Abdu’l-Bahá and several reported talks say that peace and human unity cannot be achieved without the power of the Word of God. What do the readings suggest this power adds to agreements, thought and good intentions, and where do they say it has already been seen at work?

Several passages join the Word to deeds: a sapling to be watered, a tree that must bear fruit, a dignity that must not be debased. How might a person or a community know that the Word is taking root among them?
